subject: IPM performs very differently in NIMBLE vs JAGS

messages.author: 991888581bb9f6c9
messages.subject: IPM performs very differently in NIMBLE vs JAGS
parts:
Hi all, 

Thanks to the dev team for your work on NIMBLE and everyone here for your contributions to submitted questions - I have learned a ton from monitoring this group! Today I have a question of my own to contribute. 

I am working on an integrated population model for a long-lived species. The model itself is relatively simple - m-array likelihood for adult and juvenile survival from capture-mark-resight data, binomial likelihood for productivity, and a normal observation process on population counts. The thing that I think is complicating things is that there is a relatively complex age structure. Individuals can be nearly 40 before recruiting into the breeding population, but most individuals recruit by age 15 or so. I've been experimenting with this model for a few weeks trying to get it to converge in NIMBLE, with no luck. Out of curiosity, I fit the same model in JAGS and I find the results perplexing. While JAGS mixes better, the estimates of the latent abundances especially in the matrix of immature individuals (IM[, , ]) are implausible. In contrast, in NIMBLE many of these nodes mix for a few iterations and then inexplicably stop. However, that may be acceptable as the expected value for many of these nodes is zero. Worryingly, though - many of the total abundances (N.breed.ready, N.recruits, and N.tot.breed) are not mixing at all in NIMBLE. I am writing to see if anyone has any insights into the difference in behavior of JAGS and NIMBLE here and I would love to hear suggestions with regards to how to get this thing to converge. I would prefer to fit this model in NIMBLE so that I can make use of some of the customizability as we hope to add some complexity to the model, if possible. 

I have attached a reproducible example of the same model fit in NIMBLE and JAGS, along with the necessary initial values and data objects. I have also attached traceplots of the last 2000 iterations of a 200000 iteration run in both JAGS and NIMBLE. You can see from these traceplots that JAGS and NIMBLE are sampling very different parameter spaces for the latent abundances, which leads to big differences in the estimates of total abundance. I recognize that these models are unconverged, but I would still expect them to be more similar after this many iterations, given the same model. Here is a pesky example of the same node in NIMBLE (not mixing) vs JAGS (mixing, albeit rather poorly). This result is consistent regardless of whether I use initial values or not. 




Thanks all for your insights,

Abby Bratt

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: IPM performs very differently in NIMBLE vs JAGS
parts:
Hi Abby,

Thanks for this posting.  The code and data worked and were helpful (but I added a call to set.seed for reproducibility).

I think there are a few things going on.  One is your inits$IM is not the same size as Rmodel$IM.  Did you get an obscure message about "R object of different size than NimArrDouble"?  The size mismatch in IM is generating that message.  Unfortunately it means that inits$IM is not being used. (If you didn't get that message, something might be wrong in my trying to reproduce what happened for you.) That particular message isn't very helpful because there are a lot of situations that could trigger it, most of which we hope to catch more helpfully before hitting that message, but it was a real flag that something was wrong.  I'm going to file an issue on GitHub to do more proactive error-trapping of size mismatches when setting inits and see if we can provide more useful error information.

A consequence is that after the first chain, the second chain can end up with invalid initialization and then go into catastrophic mixing, with values that are impossible in the model.  How does this happen?  The first chain doesn't get IM initialized, so the MCMC initializes it by drawing from the prior.  This seems to work in the sense that it runs and no values are invalid.  But the model then gets initialized again for the second chain.  Because inits$IM is not the right size, it is not used and the values in IM in the model remain from the end of the first chain. But other variables do get reset from inits values.  Because you have a lot of dbinom cascades, this can create impossible inits, like the dbinom outcome being larger than the number of trials (size).  Impossible inits in a complicated model structure like this can create unpredictable results.

And I think there is also an issue arising from the model structure.  It looks like there is a single sigma.obs[s, t] value for each y.count[t, s], and each sigma.obs[s,t] has an independent prior.  I think what will happen is that the mixing will find values of Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s] that exactly match y.count[t,s] and then sigma.obs[s, t] will end up at effectively 0.  At that point, I think mixing will be very stuck.  Any updates that would change Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s] will be rejected because the log prob for y.count[t,s]  will be essentially infinite (like x ~ dnorm(5, sd = 1e-10), with x = 5).  And any updates that would increase sigma.obs[s, t] will be rejected for the same reason.  If this is what's happening it might create a huge multimodality problem because *any* sets of Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s]  that match y.count[t,s]  would get locked in, or nearly locked in, in the chains.  Even if you did not monitor sigma.obs, you can check its values in the compiled model after running MCMC: Cmodel$sigma.obs. When I got things running on my system, the Cmodel$sigma.obs were all nearly 0.  For sure it is possible I was not understanding something. 

I'm guessing you ran into warnings about maximum number of contractions in the slice sampler(s), because I see you manually changed that.  It is almost always the case that that warning means something is really amiss, not just in need of an adjusted tuning parameter.  In this case it arose basically because once there were invalid values in the model, the sampler could become endlessly confused.

I hope this helps.

Perry
